cover.alt: TypeLab's letter editor in Points mode: a serif R drawn as an outline with its points

hero.alt: TypeLab's Style page: starting styles as cards that read Design everything, with filters by category and feeling beside them

blocks.heading: Context
body: TypeLab is an interactive font design playground: start from a style, reshape its proportions, shapes and details with plain-language controls, watch every letter update live, save designs to your library, and export a real .otf font.

blocks.heading: Build
body: Every design starts from one of TypeLab's own fonts, free to change, use and share under the Open Font License. Every setting reshapes their letters, and Points redraws any of them.
The settings come in three groups: proportions (weight, size and slant, heights, inner space, spacing), shapes (build and curves, corners, stroke ends) and details (letters, handwriting, effects).

blocks.alt: Choosing how strokes end: flat, flared, round, pointed and brush ends in a grid, over the preview text Design letters
Points mode: the R's outline with its points, where an edit goes to every letter shaped the same there

blocks.heading: Usability test
body: I worked through eight tasks as a first-time user would, in real Chrome, at 1440, 1024 and 390 pixels wide. The test found 13 problems: 3 high, 6 medium and 4 low.
TypeLab's core loop works: picking a style, changing it with sliders, saving and exporting a real font all succeeded. The biggest problems were about where things are, not whether they work.

images.alt: The usability test report's first page: 13 problems found, 3 high severity, 6 medium, 4 low, and all problems by severity
Problem 1 in the report: the editor doesn't fit screens narrower than about 1280 pixels

blocks.heading: What broke
body: The editor didn't fit screens narrower than about 1280 pixels, so Export was cut off on a 1024-pixel laptop and phones couldn't use it. A name change was lost if you left without pressing Save. And after you picked a style, nothing pointed to what to do next.

blocks.heading: Next
body: No real participants took part: the findings come from an expert walkthrough, so they show where people are likely to struggle. The next step is to confirm the high-severity problems with three to five real users, such as typography students or designers new to type design.

title: Clack
statement: Ten satisfying materials to pop, squish and crunch with nothing but a cursor.

cover.alt: Clack's Cyanotype: white halftone dots exposed on cobalt blue where the cursor passed

hero.alt: Clack's website: the materials side by side, Cyanotype in the middle, with Play to start a sample agent under it

blocks.heading: Why
body: We pop bubble wrap, squeeze slime and watch soap get shaved into cubes, not to finish anything but because the small, repeatable feeling settles us. ASMR videos turned these textures into a genre, and on Roblox, ASMR tower obbies have players climb from one satisfying material to the next.
On a screen, though, we mostly watch. The textures are right there, but our hands never get to touch them. What if the cursor were the fingertip?

blocks.heading: The idea
body: The screen is laid out as a grid of invisible keys. Each cell the cursor crosses is pressed once: it plays a sound, and the picture under it reacts. Slow strokes tap, fast flicks sweep, and even an idle wiggle turns into a run of sound.
No clicks, no goals, no score to lose. Each sound draws its own picture, and the picture answers where you touch it: bubbles flatten, snow takes a boot print, soap gives up a path down to the paper.

blocks.alt: Five of the materials after a stroke of the cursor: Crunchy Slime, Cyanotype, Bubble Wrap, Wax Ball and Thocky Keys
blocks.caption: 01 to 05: Crunchy Slime, Cyanotype, Bubble Wrap, Wax Ball, Thocky Keys

blocks.alt: The other five materials after a stroke of the cursor: Chewy Jellies, Pudding, Soap Cutting, Squeaky Snow and Sugar Slime
blocks.caption: 06 to 10: Chewy Jellies, Pudding, Soap Cutting, Squeaky Snow, Sugar Slime

blocks.heading: Process
body: It started as a keyboard. The first version was called ddalkkak, the Korean word for a click: a full-screen keyboard that clicked under a passing cursor, with ten sound sets and seven keycap themes. The name clack comes from there.

Once the sounds turned into wax, slime and bubble wrap, a keycap was the wrong picture for them, so each sound got a picture of its own. Most ideas didn't survive being played: the lineup shrank to Bubble Wrap and Crunchy Slime, then grew back to ten. Seventeen materials were built, played and cut along the way.

blocks.heading: What broke
body: A quick stroke can fire twenty sounds a second, so anything with a hard edge (a ring, a ping, a thump) soon sounds like gunfire. Cyanotype went from a ringing twinkle to bubble blips to soft blips, and each still sounded like shooting under a fast cursor. Filtered noise with slow attacks fixed it, and became the recipe for the calmer sounds that followed.

blocks.heading: Result
body: Clack is on the Chrome Web Store as a browser extension. It opens in the side panel beside claude.ai or ChatGPT and wakes up as an answer starts. When the answer is done, the picture fades to gray and the sound stops: your cue to go back and read it.
It only checks whether the chat is writing an answer, by its stop button. It doesn't read your messages or the answers, and it sends nothing anywhere.

images.alt: Clack in the browser's side panel beside a chat, with the line Something to clack while your chat writes
When the answer is ready, the picture in the side panel fades to gray

title: Light Life

milestones.note: Lamp · business competition win, Temple University
Lamp and website redesign · graduation show, Sejong University

statement: Lighting designed to restore natural sleep rhythms.

cover.alt: Light Life poster: the name in a warm yellow glow on black

hero.alt: Two Light Life lamps stacked, lit white and warm yellow, on a yellow to blue gradient

blocks.heading: Context
body: Light Life is a lighting system designed to support sustainable, healthier sleep in environments that often disconnect us from natural light cycles. Many people struggle to wake up or wind down due to seasonal changes, jet lag, or limited daylight exposure. Light Life addresses this by recreating the rhythm of sunlight indoors, allowing users to experience gradual changes in brightness and color that feel familiar and intuitive rather than abrupt or artificial.

The system features a dual-sided design that separates ambient and functional lighting, allowing light to influence both space and behavior. By aligning light color, intensity, and direction with human circadian patterns, the design encourages improved sleep quality within everyday living spaces.

blocks.alt: Who it's for: people aged 18 to 35, patients, and parents

blocks.heading: The lamp
body: 2023: With it, my team won the Be Your Own Boss Bowl, a business competition at Temple University.
2024: I redesigned the lamp and its website for my graduation show at Sejong University. Link it to your time zone, flip it to stack the suns and expand the light, and rotate it to color your space.

blocks.alt: Three Light Life lamps, flipped and turned different ways, under the Light Life name
Two Light Life lamps side by side, each a rounded-square head with a white light over a ribbed base

blocks.heading: The app
body: 2026: I rebuilt its app: tell it your day and your city, and it suggests the light you need.
Like the lamp, each scene has two lights, each with its own job: white sunlight that shines on you, and a color that colors your space.

blocks.heading: Reflection
